title: What the Eye Receives
logline: At a free cataract camp, dressings come off one by one, and each patient's first sight in months arrives before anyone can film their face changing.
human_question: How much of 'seeing' is a tiny patch of clouded matter, and how much is everything a person has been waiting to see again?

premise.story: A day or two at a rural eye camp, following a small number of patients from the queue through surgery to the removal of their dressings, with their full consent.
premise.place: A rural hospital or temple hall hosting a free cataract surgery camp.
premise.experience: A long, patient queue, quiet waiting, and the sudden, unrehearsed moment a dressing comes off and someone sees again.

concept_links.why: The twenty-eight kinds of matter include the sensitive matter of the eye as one small, named, failable item among many, not a guarantee. An eye camp makes visible how much of ordinary seeing depends on a tiny patch of living matter working at all.
The eye's clear sensitivity is described as a minute area, easily clouded, whose function is entirely dependent on conditions being right; cataract removal restores exactly that condition.
The sense organs are named as the most intensely 'inner' of all twenty-eight kinds of matter, the ones held most fiercely as 'mine', which is part of why their loss and recovery are so keenly felt.

what_camera_could_observe: Examinations and waiting through the day
Dressings removed, one patient at a time
What people say they missed seeing most
what_must_be_real: Full informed consent from elderly patients and their families at every stage. No 'miracle cure' framing, and no implication that clouded sight or its cause is deserved or doctrinal.

possible_arc.ending_open: Whatever a patient actually says or does first, in their own words.

requirements: A free cataract or eye camp with institutional permission to film
Patients and families giving full informed consent
A camp large enough to allow following a small number of individual stories

suggestions.name: A rural hospital or temple hall hosting a free eye camp
suggestions.why: Free eye camps are a regularly run form of rural healthcare outreach in these provinces.
suggestions.verify: A specific camp, its organisers and willing patients are unverified.

risks: Medical privacy and consent from elderly patients
Turning patients into symbols rather than people with their own reasons for coming
drop_if: No camp grants institutional permission to film
Patient consent cannot be properly and fully obtained

connections.note: Both ask what the eye actually receives, and how much of seeing is taken for granted until it fails or is questioned.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed. Everything above is a research direction.
